title: Manufacturing misallocation can rise through both margin and input-mix differences, with decline concentrated in a few industries
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper CES-26-26; U.S. manufacturing establishment data decomposing revenue-productivity dispersion into revenue-margin and input-cost-share components
geography: United States manufacturing industries and plants over the last several decades represented in the study's establishment data

observations.period: U.S. manufacturing allocative efficiency and measured misallocation; establishment study, paper published April 2026

denominator.unit: study-defined U.S. manufacturing establishment and industry analysis

components.value: dispersion in revenue margins over costs and dispersion in input cost shares contribute similarly to apparent rising misallocation

formal_link.value: the paper establishes a formal mapping between the two components and measured allocative efficiency

sector_concentration.value: rising measured misallocation is pervasive across U.S. manufacturing, but a few industries account for more than half of the aggregate decline

downstream_outcomes.unit: worker pay, employment, control, consumer prices, local capacity, and household security

observations.method: The study uses establishment data from U.S. manufacturing industries, decomposes standard revenue-productivity dispersion into revenue-margin and input-cost-share components, and maps inferred distortions to mechanisms affecting one or both components.
observations.uncertainty: Measured revenue productivity and allocative efficiency are model-dependent and are not direct measures of worker productivity, wages, firm health, consumer welfare, or public value. The abstract does not identify which policy, technology, market-power, financing, labor, or demand mechanism caused each industry's contribution.
observations.subgroup: U.S. manufacturing establishments and industries in the study period; effects may differ by industry, plant size, ownership, geography, technology, labor force, market structure, and input exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: High dispersion can reflect genuine technology, product, quality, or input differences rather than waste. A few industries' large contribution does not mean every plant in those industries is inefficient, or that reducing dispersion would automatically improve jobs, prices, or household outcomes.

related_sources.claim: Official Census PDF for CES Working Paper CES-26-26

boundary: This record adds a firm-allocation layer: aggregate productivity decline can reflect different internal distortions and can be concentrated in a small set of industries. It does not establish worker harm, consumer harm, causal policy mechanisms, local decline, or a direct path from measured misallocation to cultural or political change.
